label: The Equipment and What Each Test Measures (Lecture 20)
rows: Pulmonary function tests measure FLOW (how air moves), VOLUME (how much the lungs hold) and GAS TRANSFER (how well gas crosses into the blood).
The glass booth. Measures the total lung capacity, the functional residual capacity, the RESIDUAL VOLUME ("the key thing") and airway resistance.
Airflow and some lung volumes (handheld or desktop).
Peak expiratory flow; correlates with the forced expiratory volume in one second; bedside or home, as in asthma.
Gas exchange and oxygenation from a blood sample (pH, carbon dioxide and oxygen partial pressures, bicarbonate) · oxygen saturation and pulse rate from a fingertip clip (home use shown).
Properly calibrated equipment (the calibration syringe), clean components and correct patient technique.

label: The Four Volumes and Four Capacities
rows: "See it in your sleep." A volume is one compartment; a capacity is a SUM of volumes.
Each normal restful breath, about 500 mL.
Extra breathed IN on top of the tidal volume (3000 to 3300 mL).
Extra breathed OUT after a normal breath out.
Air left after maximal expiration; can NEVER be breathed out (1200 mL).
Expiratory reserve + residual: air left at the end of a quiet breath out, muscles relaxed (2200 to 2400 mL).
Tidal + inspiratory reserve + expiratory reserve: everything EXCEPT the residual volume (4500 to 5000 mL).
All four volumes: the maximum the lungs hold (5700 to 6200 mL).

label: Spirometry and the Forced Values
rows: Inhale maximally, then exhale forcefully, as fast as possible, for at least 6 SECONDS. Repeated 3 times; the HIGHEST volumes and flows are recorded (the slide; the recording said "average").
Total volume forcefully and rapidly exhaled after a maximal breath; reached in about 6 seconds.
Forced expiratory volume in one second
Air blown out in the FIRST SECOND.
Forced expiratory volume in one second over forced vital capacity: the % of the forced vital capacity out in the first second. Normal more than 80%; below 70% = obstruction.
The forced vital capacity, the forced expiratory volume in one second and their ratio.
Maximum velocity of forced expiration: steepest slope of the volume-time curve, top of the flow-volume loop.
Average flow over the middle half of the forced vital capacity.
Steep rise, then a plateau. Volume at 1 second = forced expiratory volume in one second; plateau = forced vital capacity.
Expiratory limb above the axis, inspiratory below; quick rise to a sharp peak, then a STRAIGHT fall to the volume axis.
Forced expiratory volume in one second and forced vital capacity 80 to 100%; total lung capacity 80 to 120%; diffusing capacity more than 60%. Ranges are given on the exam.

label: Why Order Them
rows: A pulmonary symptom: chronic shortness of breath, cough, unexplained hypercapnia or hypoxemia (smokers, occupational exposures).
They show the pathophysiological derangement and help rule out parts of the differential.
Prognosis of known disease · surgical risk before lung resection or with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
Early, asymptomatic complications of non-pulmonary disease (autoimmune disease) or of medication (long-term AMIODARONE).

label: Obstructive Against Restrictive
rows: Obstructive, restrictive and pulmonary vascular (gas transfer impairment). NOT mutually exclusive (sarcoidosis can be all three).
Increased airway resistance; trouble getting air OUT. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, ★ BRONCHIECTASIS (permanent airway dilation), cystic fibrosis.

Decrease in VOLUME; trouble getting air IN. Poor compliance (interstitial lung disease, chest wall: obesity, kyphosis, scoliosis) or neuromuscular weakness (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, muscular dystrophy).
Normal mechanics; the alveolar-capillary membrane or pulmonary blood flow. Pulmonary hypertension, chronic thromboembolic disease, early emphysema, early interstitial lung disease.
Obstruction: ratio DECREASED, below 70%. Restriction: forced vital capacity DECREASED, ratio normal or increased, 70% or more.
A slow rise and a long, late plateau (severe: no plateau, forced vital capacity reduced).
The normal shape at a LOWER volume: the air comes out easily, there is less of it.
Obstruction: the expiratory limb is concave (COVING) after the peak; severe = low peak, long flat tail.
Restriction: narrow, tall, sharp point; everything smaller; peak normal or mildly reduced, no coving.
Hyperinflated, flat diaphragms = obstruction. Small-volume lungs with reticular opacities = restriction (confirm with a low total lung capacity).

label: Reading a Report
rows: The RATIO first. 70% is your marker.
Assess the forced vital capacity: normal = obstruction; low = obstruction or MIXED (severe obstruction lowers it too); check the total lung capacity.
Assess the forced vital capacity: low = possible restriction (confirm with lung volumes); normal = normal mechanics.
Low ratio AND low total lung capacity.
Smoker: ratio 52% (low), forced vital capacity 61%, total lung capacity 120% (not low) = OBSTRUCTION, scooped loop; little change after albuterol.
Animal trainer, crackles, saturation 88%: ratio 94%, forced vital capacity 39%, total lung capacity 44% = RESTRICTION; diffusing capacity LOW (38%): the membrane is affected.
Spinal cord injury, clear lungs: ratio normal, forced vital capacity 71%, total lung capacity 67% = RESTRICTION; diffusing capacity NORMAL (97%): the membrane is intact.

label: Each Standard Test's Job, and Oxygenation
rows: Diagnose RESTRICTIVE disease (the total lung capacity confirms restriction).
Integrity of the alveolar-capillary membrane: diagnoses PULMONARY VASCULAR disease. Normal spirometry and volumes with a suspected gas transfer problem: order this next.
Airways, parenchyma, pulmonary vasculature, the bellows (diaphragm and chest wall) and the neural control of ventilation.
Arterial blood gas; exercise oximetry; six-minute walk; peak flow; maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures (diaphragmatic strength).
Walk as far as possible in 6 minutes: monitors response to treatment AND prognosis.
Oxygenation at rest and with modest activity; quick and cheap.
Pulse oximeter (fingertip) and the blood gas analyzer; the arterial blood gas is a SPECIALIZED test, not a standard one.
